questions.question: Under a Poisson change model with rate lambda, what is the probability of at least one change by time t?
options: 1 minus exp(-lambda times t)
lambda divided by t
exp(lambda plus t)
1 divided by lambda times t

questions.question: What should count as a meaningful page change?
options: Any byte difference from a rotating timestamp
A semantic content difference after controlled extraction
Every changed compression header
Only a changed URL path

questions.question: A page changes three times over 30 observed days. What is the simple raw rate estimate?
options: 0.01 per day
0.03 per day
0.10 per day
10 per day

questions.question: Why use a prior for a newly discovered page?
options: One observation proves its permanent change rate exactly
A prior makes all page classes change at the same rate
A prior eliminates the need to record fetch history
Sparse observations should be smoothed using knowledge of similar pages

questions.question: Why can weekly polling underestimate a fast page's change rate?
options: Several between-poll changes may appear as one final content difference
Every poll records all intermediate publisher versions automatically
Poisson models require pages to change only once ever
A changed content hash counts as zero observations

questions.question: Why keep both raw and semantic content hashes?
options: They guarantee semantic extraction has no parser defects
They separate transport or template changes from meaningful content changes
They remove the need for HTTP validators
They make every source timestamp trustworthy

questions.question: What does age since last successful verification do to change probability?
options: It always decreases the probability to zero
It has no role in any scheduling model
It generally increases accumulated probability that a change occurred
It converts fetch cost into document frequency

questions.question: Why divide expected stale-content benefit by fetch cost?
options: To prioritize the largest files regardless of value
To ensure every URL receives identical frequency
To ignore importance and change rate
To allocate limited capacity toward more value per resource unit

questions.question: Page A has higher importance and change rate than older Page B at equal cost. Why can A rank first?
options: Expected value depends on importance and change probability, not age alone
The oldest page must always be fetched first by definition
Change rate is ignored whenever pages have equal fetch cost
Importance affects ranking only after page content is served

questions.question: Why use a two-level host and URL scheduler?
options: To let one high-rate host monopolize all workers
To enforce host eligibility while choosing high-value URLs within it
To bypass robots and provider backoff
To convert every host into one canonical URL

questions.question: Why impose a maximum audit interval on apparently static pages?
options: To ensure static pages are fetched continuously
To remove low-rate pages permanently from scope
To prevent uncertain low estimates from starving revalidation forever
To treat every unchanged response as a server error

questions.question: A worker writes fetched content but loses its acknowledgment. How should a retry behave?
options: Create an unrelated duplicate document version
Assume the earlier write definitely failed
Delete all versions before fetching again
Use URL and content hash identity to recognize the same result

questions.question: What does an exponential recency decay with half-life h mean?
options: The recency signal halves when age reaches h
Relevance becomes zero immediately after h
Every document older than h is deleted
The query weight doubles every h days

questions.question: Why should recency not replace relevance?
options: Every information need is explicitly about the newest page
Timeless or historical queries may prefer older authoritative material
Recency cannot be computed from any timestamp
A new document is guaranteed relevant to every query

questions.question: Why is crawl time a poor default content-freshness date?
options: It always predates publication by several years
It is unavailable to acquisition systems
It changes only when semantic content changes
A newly fetched old document would appear artificially fresh

questions.topic: Recency as a Ranking Signal Fused with Relevance
questions.question: A query asks specifically about a 2024 policy. What should happen before generic newest-first boosting?
options: Apply temporal understanding or filtering for the requested effective period
Discard every 2024 document because newer always means correct
Use crawl time as the sole policy-validity date
Set recency weight to maximum for all documents

questions.question: Why evaluate recency by temporal query class?
options: A single global average exposes every evergreen regression
Freshness boosts help mutable queries but can damage evergreen and historical ones
Temporal intent never appears explicitly in query language
All query classes should use the same recency weight
